concept.name: Document Database Modeling

relationships.description: Connects Document Database Modeling to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Document database modeling optimizes for read-path locality by co-locating data that is queried together inside self-contained JSON/BSON documents, trading normalized storage for single-round-trip reads.
spark.keyTakeaway: Model documents around application access patterns rather than abstract entity-relationship tables: embed bounded 1-to-few subdocuments, reference unbounded 1-to-many arrays, and respect document size limits (e.g., MongoDB's 16 MiB BSON cap).

concept.whyItMatters: Treating a document store like MongoDB or DynamoDB as a relational database with `$lookup` joins everywhere destroys p99 latency and shards poorly. Conversely, blindly embedding unbounded arrays causes 16 MiB document overflows, write amplification, and WiredTiger cache thrashing.
whenToUse: Aggregates where parent and child data are read and mutated together in a single atomic transaction (e.g., an Order with its line items and shipping address).
Polymorphic catalog or event schemas where different item types (books, laptops, apparel) carry distinct attributes without sparse NULL columns.
Read-heavy APIs serving hierarchical JSON payloads directly from a single indexed key lookup without multi-table joins.
whenNotToUse: Highly interconnected graph or many-to-many reporting workloads requiring ad-hoc multi-hop joins across arbitrary dimensions.
Unbounded time-series or audit-log appends stored as growing arrays inside a single parent document.
Strict financial ledgers where multi-entity ACID invariants span dozens of independent aggregates on every write.
keyPoints: Embedding gives single-document atomicity and sequential disk/cache locality, ideal for 1-to-1 and bounded 1-to-few (`<100` items) relationships.
Referencing stores ObjectId/UUID foreign keys in a separate collection when child counts are unbounded (1-to-millions) or queried independently.

The **Extended Reference** pattern duplicates a small, rarely changing subset of fields (e.g., `customerName`, `customerTier`) onto the child document to eliminate cross-collection joins on hot reads.
The **Bucket Pattern** groups time-series or IoT readings into fixed-size documents (e.g., 1 hour or 200 readings per doc) to avoid millions of tiny documents and index bloat.
Every index added to a document collection speeds up reads but multiplies write IOPS and RAM footprint; indexes on multikey arrays grow proportionally with array length.

examples.title: E-commerce Product Reviews: Unbounded array refactor
examples.scenario: A product catalog stored all customer reviews inside an embedded `reviews: []` array on the `products` document. Popular items crossed 15,000 reviews, hitting MongoDB's 16 MiB BSON limit and forcing full-document rewrites on every new review.
examples.outcome: Moving reviews to a separate `reviews` collection referencing `productId` while keeping only `reviewSummary: { avgRating, count }` and the top 3 pinned reviews embedded on `products` dropped write latency from 140 ms to 4 ms and kept product docs under 12 KB.

examples.title: IoT Telemetry with the Bucket Pattern
examples.scenario: Storing 1 sensor reading per second across 10,000 devices generated 864 million documents/day, exhausting WiredTiger B-tree index memory.
examples.outcome: Bucketing 600 readings (10 minutes) per document with `minTimestamp`, `maxTimestamp`, and pre-computed `avgTemp` reduced document count by 600x, shrank index RAM by 94%, and accelerated range queries.

tradeOffs.pro: Embedding delivers single-round-trip reads and single-document ACID atomicity without distributed locks.
tradeOffs.con: Updating a duplicated embedded field (e.g., a renamed category) requires fan-out background updates across every referencing document.

tradeOffs.pro: Zero-downtime rolling deploys can introduce optional fields without `ALTER TABLE` locks.
tradeOffs.con: Unvalidated writes accumulate silent type drift (`"42"` string vs `42` int32) that breaks aggregations unless enforced via `$jsonSchema`.

tradeOffs.factor: Compound indexes vs multikey array indexes
tradeOffs.pro: A single ESR-ordered (Equality, Sort, Range) compound index covers complex queries from memory.
tradeOffs.con: Indexing large arrays generates one index entry per element, causing rapid index bloat and slower inserts.

failureModes.name: Unbounded array growth & 16 MiB overflow
failureModes.description: Pushing comments, logs, or followers into an embedded array causes documents to outgrow WiredTiger pages, fragment storage, and eventually throw `BSONObj size exceeds 16777216 bytes`.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap embedded arrays using `$slice` (Outlier/Top-N pattern) or move unbounded children to their own collection with a compound `{ parentId: 1, createdAt: -1 }` index.

failureModes.name: Working-set eviction from oversized documents
failureModes.description: Fetching a 2 MB document just to read a 200-byte status field pulls the entire 2 MB BSON blob into WiredTiger's RAM cache, evicting hot documents.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply the Subset Pattern: split heavy blobs (descriptions, full histories) into a detail collection and keep hot summary fields in the primary collection.

failureModes.name: N+1 `$lookup` join storms
failureModes.description: Running `$lookup` across unindexed foreign keys or sharded collections triggers scatter-gather queries across all shards.
failureModes.mitigation: Pre-embed immutable snapshots (e.g., `unitPrice` at order time) or maintain an Extended Reference synced via Change Streams.

failureModes.name: Hot shard key contention
failureModes.description: Choosing a monotonically increasing shard key like `createdAt` or `ObjectId` routes 100% of writes to a single shard.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a high-cardinality, evenly distributed compound shard key (e.g., `{ tenantId: 1, entityId: 1 }` or hashed key) aligned with primary query predicates.

commonMistakes: Translating a 3NF SQL ERD 1:1 into separate MongoDB collections and stitching them back together with `$lookup`.
Indexing fields in the wrong order—violating the **ESR rule** (Equality, Sort, Range)—causing in-memory sorts that hit the 100 MB sort limit.
Embedding mutable shared entities (like full `User` profiles) inside millions of `Message` documents without a fan-out update strategy.
Omitting `$jsonSchema` collection validators, allowing malformed client payloads to corrupt downstream analytics.
Using multi-document ACID transactions as a crutch for every write instead of designing single-document atomic boundaries.

sections.content:
## The idea

Relational modeling normalizes data to eliminate duplication, assuming joins are cheap and storage is expensive. **Document modeling** flips that assumption: storage is cheap, network round-trips and distributed joins are expensive, and data that is **read together should be stored together**.

In engines like MongoDB (WiredTiger) or AWS DynamoDB, a document is a self-contained tree of nested objects and arrays stored contiguously on disk. Designing a document schema starts not from an abstract list of nouns, but from your **top 5–10 read and write queries** ranked by QPS and latency SLOs.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an order-management API serving `GET /orders/:id` at 4,000 QPS:
1. **Identify access patterns**: Order detail views always need order status, shipping address, and line items (`sku`, `title`, `qty`, `unitPriceAtPurchase`). Product catalog descriptions and seller profiles are rarely needed on the order screen.
2. **Choose embedding for 1-to-few**: An order has 1–30 line items. Embed `items: [...]` directly inside the `orders` document. Because `unitPriceAtPurchase` is a historical snapshot, it never needs updating if the product's catalog price changes later.
3. **Apply Extended Reference for customer**: Embed `{ customerId, customerName }` on the order so the order list page renders without querying `customers`.
4. **Separate unbounded history**: Order audit events or shipment tracking pings go into a separate `order_events` collection indexed by `{ orderId: 1, ts: -1 }` so the `orders` document stays small (~2 KB) and cache-friendly.

edges.description: Copy immutable or low-churn fields (e.g., avgRating, customerName) onto the parent to avoid joins.

edges.description: Create { parentId: 1, createdAt: -1 } for paginated child lookups.

sections.content:
## Core design patterns for scale

- **Subset Pattern**: When a document contains a large rarely-used array (e.g., 500 historical price changes), keep only the latest 10 in the main document and archive the rest in a `*_overflow` collection. This keeps the hot working set inside WiredTiger RAM.
- **Computed Pattern**: Pre-calculate expensive aggregations (e.g., `totalOrders`, `monthlyRevenue`) incrementally via `$inc` on write rather than running `$group` across millions of documents on every dashboard load.
- **Schema Versioning Pattern**: Include `schemaVersion: 2` on every document so application readers can lazily upgrade `v1` documents in-memory without a blocking migration across 500 million rows.

## Relationship modeling matrix

| Relationship | Cardinality | Recommended Pattern | Watchout / Guardrail |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| One-to-One | `1 : 1` | Embed as subdocument | Split only if subdocument exceeds ~100 KB and is rarely read |
| One-to-Few | `1 : 2..100` | Embed as array | Enforce `$jsonSchema` `maxItems` to prevent accidental growth |
| One-to-Many | `1 : 100..100k` | Reference `parentId` on child | Always index `{ parentId: 1, sortKey: -1 }` |
| One-to-Squillions | `1 : 1M+` | Child references parent + Bucket Pattern | Never store child IDs in an array on the parent |
| Many-to-Many | `N : M` | Two-way or junction docs + Extended Ref | Keep duplicate summary fields bounded and eventually consistent |

## Failure modes

1. **16 MiB BSON ceiling crash**: Uncapped `$push` operations silently grow documents until production writes suddenly fail with `DocumentTooLarge`.
2. **Index memory starvation**: Creating 8+ secondary or multikey array indexes causes the index working set to exceed RAM, turning every write into random disk I/O.
3. **Scatter-gather shard queries**: Querying a sharded collection without the shard key in the predicate forces `mongos` to fan out to every shard, tying tail latency to the slowest shard.
4. **Write amplification on document relocation**: In storage engines or configurations where document growth forces page splits, frequent array appends fragment disk pages and spike compaction CPU.

## Indexing & query plan verification

Every critical query should be verified with `.explain("executionStats")`:
- Check that `stage` is `IXSCAN` (never `COLLSCAN`) and `totalDocsExamined` is close to `nReturned` (targeting a 1:1 ratio).
- Follow the **ESR rule**: place exact-match fields (`status: "PAID"`) first, `sort` fields (`createdAt: -1`) second, and range filters (`amount: { $gte: 50 }`) last.
- Use **partial indexes** (`partialFilterExpression: { status: "PENDING" }`) when 95% of documents are archived/completed, shrinking index size by up to 20x.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Document the top 5 read/write queries and their p99 latency targets before writing any schema.
- [ ] Embed only bounded (`<100` items) or immutable snapshot data; reference unbounded children.
- [ ] Enforce `$jsonSchema` validation and a `schemaVersion` integer on every production collection.
- [ ] Design compound indexes following Equality -> Sort -> Range (ESR) and verify `nReturned / totalDocsExamined >= 0.5` via `explain()`.
- [ ] Add partial or TTL indexes (`expireAfterSeconds`) for ephemeral sessions, OTPs, and audit logs.

interviewProblems.title: Document Database Modeling
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Document Database Modeling. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Document database modeling optimizes for read-path locality by co-locating data that is queried together inside self-contained JSON/BSON documents, trading normalized storage for single-round-trip reads.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Referenced Collection applies the primary invariant and coordinates with ESR Compound Index.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, ESR Compound Index experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap embedded arrays using `$slice` (Outlier/Top-N pattern) or move unbounded children to their own collection with a compound `{ parentId: 1, createdAt: -1 }` index.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Model documents around application access patterns rather than abstract entity-relationship tables: embed bounded 1-to-few subdocuments, reference unbounded 1-to-many arrays, and respect document size limits (e.g., MongoDB's 16 MiB BSON cap).
Avoid trap: Translating a 3NF SQL ERD 1:1 into separate MongoDB collections and stitching them back together with `$lookup`.
Avoid trap: Indexing fields in the wrong order—violating the **ESR rule** (Equality, Sort, Range)—causing in-memory sorts that hit the 100 MB sort limit.
When to reach for it: Aggregates where parent and child data are read and mutated together in a single atomic transaction (e.g., an Order with its line items and shipping address).
When to reach for it: Polymorphic catalog or event schemas where different item types (books, laptops, apparel) carry distinct attributes without sparse NULL columns.

putItTogether.title: Putting Document Database Modeling Together
putItTogether.summary: Model documents around application access patterns rather than abstract entity-relationship tables: embed bounded 1-to-few subdocuments, reference unbounded 1-to-many arrays, and respect document size limits (e.g., MongoDB's 16 MiB BSON cap).
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Document Database Modeling before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Moving reviews to a separate `reviews` collection referencing `productId` while keeping only `reviewSummary: { avgRating, count }` and the top 3 pinned reviews embedded on `products` dropped write latency from 140 ms to 4 ms and kept product docs under 12 KB.
